strengths: Novel problem formulation addressing motion-deblurred 3D human avatar reconstruction, which is practical and underexplored
Principled physics-based 3D-aware blur formation model that well-motivates the combination of SMPL and 3DGS
Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies, evaluation across blur magnitudes, and both qualitative and quantitative metrics
Significant improvements over baselines (PSNR: +2.5 on synthetic, +1.4 on real) consistently across multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS)
Valuable dataset contributions including real-captured data with 360-degree synchronized hybrid-exposure camera system
Well-structured presentation with clear figures and comprehensive ablations demonstrating component contributions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty beyond problem formulation—primarily combines existing techniques (SMPL, 3DGS, B-splines); non-rigid deformation network is generic MLP without architectural innovation
Questionable motion ambiguity resolution: inter-frame regularization (Eq. 15) is heuristic; results without it (Fig. 7) still achieve decent performance, questioning its necessity

Real dataset limited to 8 scenes with simple studio motions and only 4 blurry training views; synthetic data generated via RIFE interpolation may not reflect real optical blur; no cross-dataset evaluation
Tight coupling to auxiliary modules (SMPL, Segment-Anything masks) with no sensitivity analysis for their errors, limiting robustness and generalizability
Incomplete experimental comparisons: no direct comparisons with recent 3D-aware methods (BAD-Gaussians, BAD-NeRF) despite citing them; only compared against 2D deblurring baselines
Performance degrades significantly at higher blur levels (PSNR: 25.1 at Kblur=5 vs 24.2 at Kblur=11), suggesting limited generalization to severe blur
Key methodological details missing or unjustified: coarse initialization procedure not explained, loss function design choices lack justification, no perceptual losses included
Marginal contributions from some components: shape optimization adds only 0.046 PSNR; ablation study suggests some design choices (P, T) are not sensitive, questioning their importance

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing a genuine gap in avatar reconstruction from blurry video
Physically-grounded 3D-aware blur formation model that extends traditional 2D blur process to 3D avatar space
Sophisticated motion model combining B-spline interpolation, non-rigid deformation networks, and inter-frame regularization with thorough ablations
Contribution of both synthetic and real multi-view datasets with synchronized blurry/sharp captures to establish benchmark
Consistent quantitative improvements over baselines across metrics (PSNR +2.5-3.4 dB, LPIPS ↓0.07-0.08) with comprehensive ablation studies
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components (B-spline interpolation, deformation networks, 3DGS with SMPL) are standard techniques. Main contribution is engineering these together with a simplified blur model—primarily incremental rather than methodological advance

Oversimplified blur formation model lacking real-world physics: No rolling shutter, depth-dependent blur, lens effects, or exposure profiles. Synthetic data generation using RIFE interpolation may be circular and not reflect true motion blur

Unresolved critical limitation: Background-foreground blending during motion blur not modeled (acknowledged in Fig. 8), significantly affecting realism especially with bright backgrounds. Solution deferred to future work

Experimental design issues: (1) Unfair baseline comparisons—2D deblurring methods (RVRT, VRT, etc.) aren't designed for 3D avatar reconstruction; (2) No comparison with blur-aware 3D methods (BAD-Gaussians, BAD-NeRF); (3) Ground truth uses different camera views, not true sharp versions; (4) Limited real data (8 subjects, 4 blurry cameras)

Motion ambiguity not convincingly resolved: Simple L2 inter-frame regularization (Eq. 15) is brittle—ablation shows dramatic drops without Lreg (1.0 dB PSNR loss at non-middle timesteps). No principled solution to directional ambiguity; solution may over-constrain fast or erratic motions

Severe reproducibility gaps: Deformation network Gdisp never specified (no architecture, training, loss); Gaussian covariance initialization unclear; no training time, convergence analysis, or computational costs; SMPL calibration robustness on blurry inputs not analyzed

Missing critical comparisons with recent blur-aware 3D methods (BAD-Gaussians [76], BAD-NeRF [63]) despite their direct relevance. Authors claim these handle only camera/defocus blur, but this is not verified experimentally
Loss function oversimplified (only L1 + regularization) without perceptual losses, temporal consistency, or other modern objectives. No justification for design choices
Limited evaluation scope: No perceptual/user studies; no structural accuracy metrics (bone alignment, skinning); no animatability validation on unseen poses; no systematic failure case analysis

Strong unverified assumptions: Requires pre-computed segmentation masks (unreliable on blurry frames), SMPL calibration via EasyMoCap (robustness unclear), static cameras only, single subject only. These assumptions severely limit practical applicability

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First work to directly reconstruct sharp 3D human avatars from motion-blurred videos, with well-motivated practical relevance

Principled technical approach: Elegant 3D-aware blur formation model (Eq. 9) that naturally extends 2D blur to 3D, with thoughtful motion model combining B-spline interpolation and non-rigid deformation

Benchmark contribution: Establishes first datasets for this task with carefully designed real capture setup (hybrid-exposure 360° camera system with 4 blurry + 8 sharp cameras); code and datasets to be released

Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements across metrics (+2.5 dB PSNR synthetic, +1.4 dB real), extensive ablations isolating each component's contribution, robustness analysis across blur magnitudes
Inter-frame regularization addresses directional ambiguity: Clever design with clear motivation and effective validation demonstrating its necessity for accurate motion estimation
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale: Only 6 subjects (synthetic) and 8 scenes (real); no evaluation on diverse capture conditions, extreme motion, or different body types/clothing; no user studies for perceptual quality

Critical missing comparison: BAD-Gaussians (cited as [76], also bundle-adjusted deblur with Gaussians) not compared despite being most directly relevant recent baseline; other 3D-aware methods (BAD-NeRF, Deblur-NeRF) mentioned but not evaluated
Moderate technical novelty: Core components are existing techniques (SMPL, 3DGS, B-splines); individual component improvements modest (~0.5 dB for non-rigid model, ~0.2-0.4 dB for LBS optimization)

Fundamental limitation unresolved: Background-foreground blending caused by motion blur (Figure 8) is intrinsic to the blur model but not addressed; this could significantly impact real-world performance

Missing technical details: Sub-frame motion initialization strategy not discussed (critical for convergence); no computational cost analysis; network architecture for G_disp under-specified; SMPL initialization for blurry frames unexplained

Synthetic data concerns: Uses RIFE interpolation to generate intermediate frames, which may introduce artifacts into ground truth; real data uses only 16× exposure difference which may not reflect extreme blur scenarios
Mask dependency: Requires pre-computed segmentation masks, limiting applicability to unconstrained settings; acknowledged but unresolved

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First work to directly reconstruct sharp 3D Gaussian avatars from motion-blurred multi-view videos, addressing a practical and understudied challenge.

Principled technical approach: The 3D-aware blur formation model elegantly extends 2D blur physics to the avatar domain, with well-motivated components (B-spline interpolation, pose deformation, inter-frame regularization).

Rigorous experimental validation: Comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic (ZJU-MoCap based) and real-world datasets with custom 360° hybrid-exposure camera system; extensive ablations systematically validate each component contribution.
Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements over baselines (~2.5 dB PSNR on synthetic, ~1.4 dB on real data); qualitative results show meaningful detail recovery in body contours and textures.
Thorough robustness analysis: Systematic evaluation across blur magnitudes (Table 10), view counts (Table 13), SMPL initialization perturbations (Table 8), and mask estimation quality (Table 12).
Reproducibility commitment: Authors pledge to release code, datasets, and benchmarks, which will benefit the community and enable future research.
Practical demonstrations: iPhone 16 Pro monocular video demo shows real-world applicability beyond controlled studio settings with TRAM-based SMPL estimation.
weaknesses: Unaddressed physics approximation: Paper acknowledges real-world blur occurs in linear radiance space before ISP, but directly averages non-linear sRGB values (contradicting the physics-based framing). No experimental quantification of this approximation's impact, particularly in high-contrast regions.

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Missing comparisons with other concurrent blur-aware dynamic scene reconstruction methods (e.g., DyBlurF). The 2D-deblurring baselines were not designed for multi-view consistency, making comparisons somewhat unfair.

Fundamental SMPL dependency: Method critically depends on SMPL for all sub-frame motion. Limits applicability to loose clothing, handheld objects, and non-human elements. Performance degrades with SMPL initialization errors above ξ=0.2 (Table 8), weakening claims of robustness to coarse initialization.

Limited quantitative analysis: No motion accuracy metrics (e.g., joint angle RMSE). Novel pose evaluation (Fig. 13) is purely qualitative. Missing user studies for perceptual quality assessment. PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS are indirect measures of avatar quality.

Geometric representation limitations: 3DGS cannot recover surface normals or BRDF (acknowledged in Section 4.5.2). No comparison with geometry-aware alternatives or analysis of whether 3GS geometry is meaningful beyond rendering.
Small-scale datasets: Synthetic dataset contains only 6 subjects; real dataset only 8 scenes from controlled studio. Generalization to diverse body types, clothing, and wild motion sequences unclear.

Incomplete regularization justification: Inter-frame regularization using Geodesic distance appears ad-hoc without justification for this metric choice. Missing ablation on regularization weight λ in loss formulation (Eq. 11).
Missing computational analysis: No training time, memory usage, or inference speed reported. Practical deployment feasibility and cost comparison with baselines unavailable.
Hyperparameter design not fully justified: Virtual image count T=5 chosen empirically (Table 7) without principled justification. No adaptive blur magnitude estimation to adjust T per-video.

Loss function underspecified: Only L1 + L_reg used. No exploration or justification against perceptual losses, adversarial losses, or other alternatives that might improve quality metrics beyond PSNR.

strengths: Well-motivated novel problem: First work to address blur-aware 3D human avatar reconstruction with clear articulation of why 2D deblurring + 3D reconstruction fails
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Extensive ablation studies across components, blur magnitudes, view numbers, mask quality, and initialization perturbations
Real-world dataset contribution: Custom 360-degree hybrid-exposure camera system with synchronized captures addresses lack of benchmarks for this task
Quantitative improvements: Consistent gains over baselines across metrics (PSNR +2.5 on synthetic, +1.4 on real; SSIM, LPIPS improvements)
Physically-motivated technical approach: 3D blur formation framework (Eq. 3) extends traditional 2D blur into 3D space in a principled way
Clear presentation of problem ambiguities: Figure 1 effectively illustrates motion-induced blur ambiguities that motivate the approach
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Method primarily combines established techniques (B-spline interpolation, CNN pose deformation, LBS refinement) without fundamental algorithmic contributions
Critical SMPL dependency: Cannot handle handheld objects, loose garments, or independent clothing motion; Table 9 shows dramatic performance drop without SMPL optimization (PSNR 21.63 vs 25.55)
Under-specified technical details: Loss weighting between L1 and Lreg not specified; coarse initialization method not explained; no training time or computational cost analysis

Missing key experiments: No user study to validate perceptual quality improvements; recent blur-aware methods (BARD-GS, DyBlurF) cited but not experimentally compared; only qualitative novel-view results
Limited dataset diversity: Synthetic data from only 6 ZJU-MoCap subjects; real dataset with 8 scenes insufficient for demonstrating generalization across body types and clothing
Questionable baseline performance: 2D deblurring baselines marginally outperform direct training on blurry data—unclear if methods were properly tuned or comparison is fair

Insufficient generalization evidence: Performance degrades significantly with fewer views (Table 13: PSNR 23.33 with 2 views vs 25.55 with 4); iPhone demo qualitative only; no diverse body/pose testing
Physical accuracy unaddressed: Acknowledged that averaging non-linear sRGB values causes high-contrast inaccuracies; cannot recover accurate geometry—these limitations remain unaddressed

Incomplete ablation studies: No isolated ablation of 3D-aware formulation benefit; hyperparameter sensitivity (P, T) explored cursorily; no loss weight sensitivity analysis; B-spline+CNN design choice unjustified
Initialization sensitivity: Table 8 shows non-trivial sensitivity to pose perturbations (PSNR drops to 25.14 with ξ=0.4); critical for ill-posed problem but under-analyzed

Technical concerns: Polynomial basis for SO(3) rotation interpolation (Eq. 4) is unconventional; relative loss weighting unexplained; pose deformation model rationale unclear versus end-to-end trajectory learning

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem addressing a practical gap in avatar reconstruction: existing methods require sharp input, but motion blur is common in real scenarios
Sound technical approach with logical extension of 2D blur to 3D-aware model (Eq. 3) using SMPL and B-spline motion interpolation
Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple metrics (PSNR +2.5-3.9dB over baselines, LPIPS improvements 33-35%) on both synthetic and real data
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including thorough ablations (Tables 3-8), robustness studies to SMPL initialization and mask quality, and evaluation across blur magnitudes and view counts

Valuable benchmark contributions: synthetic dataset (ZJU-MoCap derived) and high-quality real-world dataset with carefully synchronized 360° hybrid-exposure capture system; promise to release code/data
Excellent presentation with clear figures (especially Figures 1-2) that effectively motivate the problem; well-organized method and results sections
Demonstrated robustness to coarse SMPL initialization (Table 8) and generalization to monocular iPhone capture, showing practical applicability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: B-spline pose interpolation is well-established (De Boor-Cox), SMPL and 3DGS are existing representations; novelty primarily lies in problem formulation rather than methodological innovation

Missing quantitative comparisons with recent blur-aware 3D methods (BARD-GS, DyBlurF mentioned in related work but not evaluated), raising questions about relative performance against directly comparable approaches
Fundamental dependence on SMPL representation limits generality: cannot handle handheld objects or loose garments; applicability restricted to standard human poses without accessories

Unaddressed synthetic-to-real gap: real-world blur occurs in linear radiance space before ISP, but method averages non-linear sRGB values; synthetic blur uses frame interpolation which may not match physical camera blur

Incomplete technical specification of key components: pose deformation network Gdisp architecture, training details, and initialization scheme not clearly described; LBS offset prediction network similarly underspecified
Geometry and BRDF recovery limitations acknowledged but unresolved: method produces texture but not true 3D geometry or surface properties; important for complete avatar reconstruction
Computational cost not reported: no training time, inference speed, or memory requirements provided; essential practical information missing

Small real-world dataset (8 scenes) limits validation of generalization; ground truth uses separately-captured sharp frames from 8 different cameras rather than ideally synchronized same-viewpoint captures
Incomplete ablation studies: no architectural ablations for displacement and LBS networks; no systematic analysis of which motion types are well/poorly handled; limited failure case characterization

Loss function design underspecified: simple L1 without perceptual losses; uniform joint weighting in regularization (Eq. 9) may not reflect differential importance; choice of T=5 interpolation frames not justified
